claim: Autoreactive thymocytes are eliminated during negative selection in the thymus.
source: Autoreactive thymocytes are eliminated during negative selection in the thymus, a process important for establishing self-tolerance.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in immunology presented in the abstract.

claim: Negative selection is important for establishing self-tolerance.
source: Autoreactive thymocytes are eliminated during negative selection in the thymus, a process important for establishing self-tolerance.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the abstract.

claim: Phagocytosis promotes negative selection.
source: Here, using a murine thymic slice model in which thymocytes undergo negative selection in situ, we demonstrate that phagocytosis promotes negative selection
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Autoreactive CD8 T cells can escape to the periphery when phagocytosis in the thymus is impaired.
source: Here, using a murine thymic slice model in which thymocytes undergo negative selection in situ, we demonstrate that phagocytosis promotes negative selection, and provide evidence for the escape of autoreactive CD8 T cells to the periphery when phagocytosis in the thymus is impaired.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing increased activated CD8 T cells in Tim-4 deficient mice.

claim: Negative selection is more efficient when the phagocyte also presents the negative selecting peptide.
source: We also show that negative selection is more efficient when the phagocyte also presents the negative selecting peptide.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data with bone marrow-derived dendritic cells.

claim: The death process initiated following strong TCR signaling is facilitated by phagocytosis.
source: Our findings support a model for negative selection in which the death process initiated following strong TCR signaling is facilitated by phagocytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The phagocytic capability of cells that present self-peptides is a key determinant of thymocyte fate.
source: Thus, the phagocytic capability of cells that present self-peptides is a key determinant of thymocyte fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Thymocytes bearing self-reactive T cell receptors (TCR) are eliminated from the T cell repertoire during negative selection.
source: During negative selection, thymocytes bearing self-reactive T cell receptors (TCR) are eliminated from the T cell repertoire, an important process for the establishment of self-tolerance.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: Thymocytes bearing TCRs with high affinity for self-ligands can receive apoptotic death signals.
source: Thymocytes interact with a variety of thymic-resident cells that present self-peptide:MHC complexes, and thymocytes bearing TCRs with high affinity for self-ligands can receive apoptotic death signals (Starr et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Apoptosis is an immunologically silent form of cell death that is generally thought to be cell-autonomous once initiated.
source: Apoptosis is an immunologically silent form of cell death that is generally thought to be cell-autonomous once initiated (Strasser et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Hematopoietic cells, especially dendritic cells (DC), are potent inducers of negative selection.
source: For example, hematopoietic cells, especially dendritic cells (DC), are potent inducers of negative selection, whereas cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTEC) are specialized to mediate positive selection, promoting thymocyte maturation and survival (Gallegos and Bevan, 2004; Klein et al., 2014; McCaughtry et al., 2008; Ohnmacht et al., 2009; Proietto et al., 2008; Taniguchi et al., 2012; Wirasinha et al., 2019; Yap et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTEC) are specialized to mediate positive selection, promoting thymocyte maturation and survival.
source: For example, hematopoietic cells, especially dendritic cells (DC), are potent inducers of negative selection, whereas cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTEC) are specialized to mediate positive selection, promoting thymocyte maturation and survival (Gallegos and Bevan, 2004; Klein et al., 2014; McCaughtry et al., 2008; Ohnmacht et al., 2009; Proietto et al., 2008; Taniguchi et al., 2012; Wirasinha et al., 2019; Yap et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The death of autoreactive thymocytes invariably occurred during close contact with phagocytes.
source: In particular, visualization of dying thymocytes and phagocytes within thymic tissue slices showed that the death of autoreactive thymocytes invariably occurred during close contact with phagocytes, and in most cases death appeared to occur after phagocytosis (Dzhagalov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: In most cases, thymocyte death appeared to occur after phagocytosis.
source: In particular, visualization of dying thymocytes and phagocytes within thymic tissue slices showed that the death of autoreactive thymocytes invariably occurred during close contact with phagocytes, and in most cases death appeared to occur after phagocytosis (Dzhagalov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Dendritic cells are the most potent antigen-presenting cells (APC) for priming naïve T cells.
source: Dendritic cells are the most potent antigen-presenting cells (APC) for priming naïve T cells and also present self-peptide for negative selection (Gallegos and Bevan, 2004; McCaughtry et al., 2008; Norbury et al., 2002; Ohnmacht et al., 2009; Proietto et al., 2008; Taniguchi et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Dendritic cells present self-peptide for negative selection.
source: Dendritic cells are the most potent antigen-presenting cells (APC) for priming naïve T cells and also present self-peptide for negative selection (Gallegos and Bevan, 2004; McCaughtry et al., 2008; Norbury et al., 2002; Ohnmacht et al., 2009; Proietto et al., 2008; Taniguchi et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Thymic macrophages are known for their role in clearing away apoptotic thymocytes.
source: whereas thymic macrophages are known for their role in clearing away apoptotic thymocytes (Surh and Sprent, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phagocytes recognize and uptake apoptotic cells via receptors for 'eat-me' signals displayed on the surface of dying cells.
source: Phagocytes recognize and uptake apoptotic cells via receptors for 'eat-me' signals displayed on the surface of dying cells (Arandjelovic and Ravichandran, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Apoptosis induces asymmetry in the plasma membrane, leading to the exposure of phosphatidylserine (PS).
source: For example, apoptosis induces asymmetry in the plasma membrane, leading to the exposure of phosphatidylserine (PS), which is then recognized by PS receptors on phagocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Phosphatidylserine (PS) is recognized by PS receptors on phagocytes.
source: For example, apoptosis induces asymmetry in the plasma membrane, leading to the exposure of phosphatidylserine (PS), which is then recognized by PS receptors on phagocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: A variety of 'eat-me' receptors are expressed and functional in the thymus.
source: A variety of 'eat-me' receptors are expressed and functional in the thymus (Elliott et al., 2009; Miyanishi et al., 2007; Tacke et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Treatment of thymic slices for 16 hr of culture with AP20187 led to the depletion of approximately 50% of F4/80hi macrophages and CD11chi DC in MAFIA, but not WT, thymic slices.
source: We observed that treatment of thymic slices for 16 hr of culture with AP20187 led to the depletion of approximately 50% of F4/80hi macrophages and CD11chi DC in MAFIA, but not WT, thymic slices (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: On phagocyte-depleted slices (MAFIA+AP20187) containing OVAp, the ratio of live OT-I:reference thymocytes was similar to that in control slices without antigen.
source: In contrast, on phagocyte-depleted slices (MAFIA+AP20187) containing OVAp, the ratio of live OT-I:reference thymocytes was similar to that in control slices without antigen, consistent with the idea that phagocytes promote negative selection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: OT-I thymocytes on phagocyte-depleted slices did not show decreased levels of the TCR activation marker CD69.
source: However, OT-I thymocytes on phagocyte-depleted slices did not show decreased levels of the TCR activation marker CD69, indicating that surviving thymocytes had received strong TCR signals, in spite of phagocyte depletion (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Thymocytes on phagocyte-depleted thymic slices exhibit enhanced survival despite continuing to receive strong TCR signals.
source: These results suggest that thymocytes on phagocyte-depleted thymic slices exhibit enhanced survival despite continuing to receive strong TCR signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: In RIPmOVA transgenic mice, the model antigen ovalbumin (OVA) is expressed in a subset of medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs).
source: In RIPmOVA transgenic mice, the model antigen ovalbumin (OVA), which provides the agonist peptide for OT-I thymocytes, is expressed in a subset of medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs), and is presented in the medulla by mTECs and hematopoietic-derived cells (Gallegos and Bevan, 2004; Kurts et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In RIPmOVA transgenic mice, OVA is presented in the medulla by mTECs and hematopoietic-derived cells.
source: In RIPmOVA transgenic mice, the model antigen ovalbumin (OVA), which provides the agonist peptide for OT-I thymocytes, is expressed in a subset of medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs), and is presented in the medulla by mTECs and hematopoietic-derived cells (Gallegos and Bevan, 2004; Kurts et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Approximately 50% of CD4+CD8+ double positive thymocytes from OT-I mice express a medullary chemokine receptor pattern (CXCR4-CCR7+).
source: Because approximately 50% of CD4+CD8+ double positive thymocytes, and all of the more mature CD8+ single positive thymocytes from OT-I mice express a medullary chemokine receptor pattern (CXCR4-CCR7+) and migrate to the medulla in thymic slices (Ehrlich et al., 2009; Halkias et al., 2013; Kurd and Robey, 2016; Yin et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: All of the more mature CD8+ single positive thymocytes from OT-I mice express a medullary chemokine receptor pattern (CXCR4-CCR7+) and migrate to the medulla in thymic slices.
source: Because approximately 50% of CD4+CD8+ double positive thymocytes, and all of the more mature CD8+ single positive thymocytes from OT-I mice express a medullary chemokine receptor pattern (CXCR4-CCR7+) and migrate to the medulla in thymic slices (Ehrlich et al., 2009; Halkias et al., 2013; Kurd and Robey, 2016; Yin et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Approximately 50% of OT-I thymocytes were lost by 9 hr on RIPmOVA slices, and there was no further reduction through 48 hr of culture.
source: We observed that approximately 50% of OT-I thymocytes were lost by 9 hr, and there was no further reduction through 48 hr of culture (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Cell death occurred while thymocytes were in close contact with, or engulfed by, GFP-expressing phagocytes.
source: Consistent with our earlier study (Dzhagalov et al., 2013), cell death occurred while thymocytes were in close contact with, or engulfed by, GFP-expressing phagocytes (Figure 2b, Videos 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b and Videos 1-2.

claim: The close coupling of autoreactive thymocyte death and phagocytosis occurs during negative selection to both tissue-restricted and ubiquitous self-antigen.
source: Thus, the close coupling of autoreactive thymocyte death and phagocytosis occurs during negative selection to both tissue-restricted and ubiquitous self-antigen.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing RIPmOVA and peptide-induced models.

claim: Negative selection on RIPmOVA thymic slices was completely blocked by treatment of thymic slices with AnnV.
source: Negative selection on RIPmOVA thymic slices was completely blocked by treatment of thymic slices with AnnV (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: CD69 upregulation on surviving thymocytes was not impaired by AnnV treatment.
source: This was not due to a failure of thymocytes to receive strong TCR signals, since CD69 upregulation on surviving thymocytes was not impaired (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: AnnV addition had a similar effect on negative selection in response to OVAp.
source: AnnV addition had a similar effect on negative selection in response to OVAp (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: Phagocytosis promotes the death of autoreactive thymocytes.
source: These results confirm that phagocytosis promotes the death of autoreactive thymocytes, and suggest that PS receptors are important for this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AnnV blocking experiments.

claim: PS receptors are important for the death of autoreactive thymocytes.
source: These results confirm that phagocytosis promotes the death of autoreactive thymocytes, and suggest that PS receptors are important for this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AnnV blocking experiments.

claim: Tim-4 is expressed by almost all F4/80hi macrophages and ~30% of CD11chi DCs.
source: Using flow cytometry, we found that Tim-4 is expressed by almost all F4/80hi macrophages and ~30% of CD11chi DCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: OT-I thymocyte death was not detectable in Timd4-/- RIPmOVA thymic slices.
source: OT-I thymocyte death was not detectable in Timd4-/- RIPmOVA thymic slices, but was readily detectable in thymic slices from age and sex-matched Timd4+/+ RIPmOVA controls (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Negative selection in response to OVAp was slightly reduced on Timd4-/- thymic slices, although the difference did not reach statistical significance.
source: Negative selection in response to OVAp was also slightly reduced on Timd4-/- thymic slices, although the difference did not reach statistical significance (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Normal CD69 upregulation by OT-I thymocytes suggested that surviving thymocytes received strong TCR signals, even when OVA is presented in the Timd4-/- thymic environment.
source: Normal CD69 upregulation by OT-I thymocytes suggested that surviving thymocytes received strong TCR signals, even when OVA is presented in the Timd4-/- thymic environment (Figure 4b,d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b,d.

claim: Tim-4 is a relevant player in negative selection.
source: Taken together, these data support the idea that phagocytosis promotes effective negative selection, and suggest that Tim-4 is a relevant player in this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Tim-4 knockout experiments.

claim: There is an increase in CD8 T cells with an activated phenotype (CD44hiCD62Llo) in mature CD8 T cells in the spleens of Timd4-/- mice.
source: Consistent with this, we observed an increase in CD8 T cells with an activated phenotype (CD44hiCD62Llo) in mature CD8 T cells in the spleens of Timd4-/- mice (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: There is a reproducible increase in the level of Ki67 expression amongst 'Ki67lo' CD8 T cells derived from thymocytes of Timd4-/- mice.
source: While the phenotype of T cells, including the proportion of dividing cells (Ki67hi), derived from Timd4-/- versus wild type mice were similar (Figure 5b,c and data not shown), we noted a reproducible increase in the level of Ki67 expression amongst 'Ki67lo' CD8 T cells derived from thymocytes of Timd4-/- mice (Figure 5b,d) indicative of more rapid transit through G0 (Hogan et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2018; Sobecki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b,d.

claim: Increased Ki67 expression in Ki67lo CD8 T cells is indicative of more rapid transit through G0.
source: While the phenotype of T cells, including the proportion of dividing cells (Ki67hi), derived from Timd4-/- versus wild type mice were similar (Figure 5b,c and data not shown), we noted a reproducible increase in the level of Ki67 expression amongst 'Ki67lo' CD8 T cells derived from thymocytes of Timd4-/- mice (Figure 5b,d) indicative of more rapid transit through G0 (Hogan et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2018; Sobecki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The increase in activated CD8 T cells in intact Timd4-/- mice is consistent with increased self-reactivity of CD8 T cells.
source: This difference, which was also apparent in the blood of steady-state Timd4-/- animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), together with the increase in activated CD8 T cells in intact Timd4-/- mice (Figure 5a), is consistent with increased self-reactivity of CD8 T cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: These differences in CD8 T cells were not observed amongst CD4 T cells.
source: Interestingly, these differences were not observed amongst CD4 T cells (Figure 5a,d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a,d.

claim: Defective phagocytosis in the thymus of Timd4-/- mice leads to the escape of CD8 T cells with borderline self-reactivity.
source: These data suggest that defective phagocytosis in the thymus of Timd4-/- mice leads to the escape of CD8 T cells with borderline self-reactivity, and support the idea that Tim-4-mediated phagocytosis in the thymus facilitates efficient negative selection of CD8 T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on CD8 T cells from Tim-4 deficient mice.

claim: Tim-4-mediated phagocytosis in the thymus facilitates efficient negative selection of CD8 T cells.
source: These data suggest that defective phagocytosis in the thymus of Timd4-/- mice leads to the escape of CD8 T cells with borderline self-reactivity, and support the idea that Tim-4-mediated phagocytosis in the thymus facilitates efficient negative selection of CD8 T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on CD8 T cells from Tim-4 deficient mice.

claim: OVA-loaded WT DCs induced a significant level of negative selection.
source: Interestingly, while OVA-loaded WT DCs induced a significant level of negative selection, Timd4-/- DCs failed to induce detectable negative selection (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Timd4-/- DCs failed to induce detectable negative selection.
source: Interestingly, while OVA-loaded WT DCs induced a significant level of negative selection, Timd4-/- DCs failed to induce detectable negative selection (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The defect in negative selection by Timd4-/- DCs was not due to defective peptide presentation.
source: This defect was not due to defective peptide presentation by Timd4-/- DCs, as surviving OT-I thymocytes strongly upregulated CD69 in the presence of OVA-loaded Timd4-/- DCs (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Peptide-presenting cells defective in phagocytosis were unable to effectively induce negative selection, despite the fact that functional (non-presenting) endogenous phagocytes were present in the thymic slice.
source: The fact that peptide-presenting cells defective in phagocytosis were unable to effectively induce negative selection, despite the fact that functional (non-presenting) endogenous phagocytes were present in the thymic slice, indicates that negative selection is more efficient when the same cell serves both as APC and phagocyte.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BMDC experiments.

claim: Negative selection is more efficient when the same cell serves both as APC and phagocyte.
source: The fact that peptide-presenting cells defective in phagocytosis were unable to effectively induce negative selection, despite the fact that functional (non-presenting) endogenous phagocytes were present in the thymic slice, indicates that negative selection is more efficient when the same cell serves both as APC and phagocyte.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BMDC experiments.

claim: Phagocytes mediate thymocyte death directly via phagocytosis.
source: Although indirect mechanisms such as retinoic acid and cytokine production by phagocytes (Sarang et al., 2013) and PS signaling (Elliott et al., 2005), might also impact thymocyte survival, the fact that we observe similar defects in negative selection upon phagocyte depletion, blocking PS, and mutation of a PS receptor, strongly suggests that phagocytes mediate thymocyte death directly via phagocytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results.

claim: The phagocytic activity of a peptide-presenting cell is a key factor in determining thymocyte fate.
source: Our observation that negative selection is most efficient when phagocytes also serve as peptide-presenting cells implies that the phagocytic activity of a peptide-presenting cell is a key factor in determining thymocyte fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The inability to phagocytose could help to explain the relative inefficiency of thymic stromal cells to induce negative selection.
source: Indeed, the inability to phagocytose could help to explain the relative inefficiency of thymic stromal cells to induce negative selection (McCaughtry et al., 2008; Melichar et al., 2013; Ohnmacht et al., 2009; Proietto et al., 2008; Wirasinha et al., 2019; Yap et al., 2018), in contrast to the phagocytic activity of many hematopoietic cells which are potent inducers of negative selection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and supported by citations.

claim: A subset of thymic hematopoietic cells with characteristics of both DCs and macrophages may be particularly important mediators of negative selection.
source: Thus, a subset of thymic hematopoietic cells with characteristics of both DCs and macrophages may be particularly important mediators of negative selection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that many thymic phagocytes express both LysM-GFP and CD11c.

claim: Mutation of Tim-4 impaired negative selection to TRA, but had a less obvious impact on negative selection to exogenously added antigenic peptide.
source: We found that mutation of a single PS receptor, Tim-4, impaired negative selection to TRA, but had a less obvious impact on negative selection to exogenously added antigenic peptide.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings comparing RIPmOVA and peptide-induced models in Tim-4 knockout mice.

claim: Globally blocking PS significantly impaired both forms of negative selection (TRA and ubiquitous antigen).
source: On the other hand, globally blocking PS significantly impaired both forms of negative selection.
evidence: This is a summary of the AnnV blocking experiments.

claim: Tim-4 plays a non-redundant role in phagocytosis in the medulla.
source: These results could indicate that Tim-4 plays a non-redundant role in phagocytosis in the medulla, the site of TRA presentation, whereas other PS receptors may participate in phagocytosis in the thymic cortex, where negative selection to ubiquitous antigen takes place (Daley et al., 2013; Klein et al., 2014; McCaughtry et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential effects of Tim-4 mutation on TRA vs ubiquitous antigen negative selection.

claim: Other PS receptors may participate in phagocytosis in the thymic cortex, where negative selection to ubiquitous antigen takes place.
source: These results could indicate that Tim-4 plays a non-redundant role in phagocytosis in the medulla, the site of TRA presentation, whereas other PS receptors may participate in phagocytosis in the thymic cortex, where negative selection to ubiquitous antigen takes place (Daley et al., 2013; Klein et al., 2014; McCaughtry et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Negative selection to TRA might be more sensitive to perturbations in phagocytosis than negative selection to ubiquitous antigen.
source: Alternatively, negative selection to TRA might be more sensitive to perturbations in phagocytosis, given that TRA are typically expressed at low levels, and may deliver a relatively weak apoptotic signal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the differential effects of Tim-4 mutation.

claim: Cells receiving a weak apoptotic signal in C. elegans embryos are more dependent upon phagocytosis for their death than cells receiving a strong apoptotic signal.
source: In line with this idea, cells receiving a weak apoptotic signal in C. elegans embryos are more dependent upon phagocytosis for their death than cells receiving a strong apoptotic signal (Hoeppner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phagocytes might be especially critical during negative selection to relatively low-affinity or rare self-antigens.
source: This raises the intriguing possibility that phagocytes might be especially critical during negative selection to relatively low-affinity or rare self-antigens, which pose the greatest risk as targets of autoimmunity (Koehli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: A requirement for Tim-4 in negative selection involving relatively weak apoptotic stimuli is consistent with the mild autoimmune phenotype reported in Timd4-/- mice.
source: A requirement for Tim-4 in negative selection involving relatively weak apoptotic stimuli is consistent with the mild autoimmune phenotype reported in Timd4-/- mice (Rodriguez-Manzanet et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CD8 T cells that developed in a thymic environment lacking Tim-4, but then further matured in a Tim-4 sufficient peripheral environment, exhibited slightly elevated levels of Ki67.
source: Specifically, we observed that CD8 T cells that developed in a thymic environment lacking Tim-4, but then further matured in a Tim-4 sufficient peripheral environment, exhibited slightly elevated levels of Ki67.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Ki67 decays slowly after cell division, and thus can serve as measure of time spent in G0.
source: Although Ki67 is widely used as a binary marker of cell proliferation, recent studies indicate that Ki67 decays slowly after cell division, and thus can serve as measure of time spent in G0 (Hogan et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2018; Sobecki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CD8 T cells from intact Timd4-/- mice exhibit slightly elevated levels of Ki67 and have an increased proportion of cells with an activated phenotype.
source: In addition, CD8 T cells from intact Timd4-/- mice also exhibit slightly elevated levels of Ki67 and have an increased proportion of cells with an activated phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: These changes in CD8 T cells are consistent with increased homeostatic proliferation characteristic of T cells with elevated self-reactivity.
source: These changes are consistent with increased homeostatic proliferation characteristic of T cells with elevated self-reactivity (Ge et al., 2004; Ge et al., 2001; Hogan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Thymocyte death has a larger impact on the CD8, compared to the CD4, T cell lineage.
source: This is consistent with evidence that thymocyte death has a larger impact on the CD8, compared to the CD4, T cell lineage (Sinclair et al., 2013) and the relatively modest role of deletion in maintaining tolerance within CD4 lineage T cells, due to the diversion of self-reactive CD4 T cells into the regulatory T cell lineage (Legoux et al., 2015; Malhotra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Deletion plays a relatively modest role in maintaining tolerance within CD4 lineage T cells, due to the diversion of self-reactive CD4 T cells into the regulatory T cell lineage.
source: This is consistent with evidence that thymocyte death has a larger impact on the CD8, compared to the CD4, T cell lineage (Sinclair et al., 2013) and the relatively modest role of deletion in maintaining tolerance within CD4 lineage T cells, due to the diversion of self-reactive CD4 T cells into the regulatory T cell lineage (Legoux et al., 2015; Malhotra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Timd4-/- mice do not develop overt autoimmunity, likely due to the presence of other tolerance mechanisms.
source: Notably, Timd4-/- mice do not develop overt autoimmunity, likely due to the presence of other tolerance mechanisms, such as regulatory T cells and peripheral tolerance mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotype and knowledge of tolerance mechanisms.

claim: Thymic dendritic cells that provide both high-affinity TCR ligands and a local source of IL-2 can efficiently support the development of regulatory T cells.
source: We recently reported that thymic dendritic cells that provide both high-affinity TCR ligands and a local source of IL-2 can efficiently support the development of regulatory T cells (Klein et al., 2018; Weist et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The decision of an autoreactive thymocyte to die or differentiate may ultimately depend on whether it engages a peptide-presenting cell that promotes its death or supports its further development.
source: Thus, the decision of an autoreactive thymocyte to die or differentiate may ultimately depend on whether it engages a peptide-presenting cell that promotes its death or supports its further development.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: GFP-expressing cells in LysMGFP reporter mice include a subset of F4/80hi macrophages that have been previously described as having potent phagocytic abilities.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of the thymus of LysMGFP mice revealed that GFP-expressing cells include a subset of F4/80hi macrophages that have been previously described as having potent phagocytic abilities, as well as a subset of CD11chi DCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Dzhagalov et al., 2013; Tacke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: GFP-expressing cells in LysMGFP reporter mice include a subset of CD11chi DCs.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of the thymus of LysMGFP mice revealed that GFP-expressing cells include a subset of F4/80hi macrophages that have been previously described as having potent phagocytic abilities, as well as a subset of CD11chi DCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Dzhagalov et al., 2013; Tacke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: The MAFIA transgene is expressed in F4/80hi macrophages and CD11chi DCs.
source: We confirmed expression of the MAFIA transgene in these subsets using flow cytometric analysis to measure expression of a linked GFP gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (DCs) have phagocytic activity.
source: To test this idea, we took advantage of the fact that bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (DCs) have phagocytic activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and can serve as exogenous peptide presenting cells when overlaid and allowed to migrate into thymic slices (Melichar et al., 2013; Weist et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: Bone marrow-derived dendritic cells can serve as exogenous peptide presenting cells when overlaid and allowed to migrate into thymic slices.
source: To test this idea, we took advantage of the fact that bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (DCs) have phagocytic activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and can serve as exogenous peptide presenting cells when overlaid and allowed to migrate into thymic slices (Melichar et al., 2013; Weist et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The early events associated with apoptosis are not necessarily a death sentence.
source: In vitro studies of apoptosis support a model in which a death signal initiates a cell-autonomous program of cellular destruction involving protease and nuclease activation, PS exposure on the outer membrane, membrane blebbing, and the formation of apoptotic bodies (Strasser et al., 2000). Our current work adds to a growing body of evidence that the early events associated with apoptosis are not necessarily a death sentence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study and supported by citation.

claim: Activated T cells can transiently express active caspase-3 and expose PS at the cell surface, but ultimately avoid cell death.
source: For example, activated T cells can transiently express active caspase-3 and expose PS at the cell surface, but ultimately avoid cell death (Alam et al., 1999; Elliott et al., 2005; Fischer et al., 2006; McComb et al., 2010; Miossec et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Phagocyte-dependent killing is critical for regulating the size of T cell, erythrocyte, and neutrophil populations.
